subject: Business Models
title: Forking a Platform
description: A quick, practical guide to Forking a Platform.

hook.text: Amazon took Android's open-source code, removed Google's services, and created its own Fire OS.

buildup.text: Forking means taking an open platform's code and creating an independent version. Legal but aggressive.

discovery.text: Android's open-source license allows this. Google fights back by keeping its best apps proprietary.

twist.text: China's entire Android ecosystem is forked. No Google services—Huawei, Xiaomi, and others run their own.

climax.text: Forking tests platform resilience. If the best features are open, competitors can clone your platform.

punchline.text: Open enough to grow, closed enough to defend. The platform dilemma.

quiz.question: Why did Amazon fork Android?
options: To create an independent ecosystem without Google

details.summary: Forking occurs when participants take a platform's open-source code, data, or community and create a competing version. Android was forked from open-source Linux. LibreOffice forked from OpenOffice. Forks can split communities or create specialized alternatives.
details.whyItMatters: Fork risk constrains platform behavior because open-source platforms and protocol-based networks can be duplicated. Understanding fork dynamics helps explain why some platforms remain open while others build proprietary walls.
takeaways: Open-source platforms can be copied and modified by anyone
Forks succeed when the original platform alienates its community
Fork risk incentivizes platforms to keep communities satisfied

faq.question: When do platform forks succeed versus fail?
faq.answer: Forks succeed when the original platform makes unpopular decisions like changing licenses, raising prices, or ignoring community needs. They fail when the network effects of the original are too strong and the forked community is too small to be self-sustaining.

faq.question: How do proprietary platforms prevent forking?
faq.answer: Closed-source code cannot be forked. Proprietary data formats create lock-in. Terms of service prohibit data export. API dependencies ensure functionality requires the original platform. These strategies prevent forking but also invite regulatory scrutiny.
